message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study

The study has two errors that change its conclusions, and the funding and capacity claims are not supported as written. Recommendation 7 should not go to Cabinet in its current form.

## Critical issues

**1. The "broadly similar participation" claim contradicts Table 1 (Section 2).**
Houses participate at 66% and flats at 21%, so flat participation is less than a third of the house rate. The conclusion that the service can be "rolled out uniformly... without a separate approach for flats" has no support, and the data points the other way. Flats make up about 10,400 district households, so this matters. The study should either propose a flats-specific approach (communal bins, different caddies, targeted engagement) or cost the low participation explicitly.

**2. The district projection uses the wrong participation rate (Section 3).**
The text cites a "64%" pilot participation rate, but Table 1 gives 57%. The 3,290 tonnes figure only works with 64% (52,000 × 0.64 × 1.9 kg × 52 ≈ 3,288 t).
- Using the pilot's 57%, the projection is about **2,930 tonnes**.
- Applying the house and flat rates and yields separately gives about **2,870 tonnes**. The pilot's 20% flat share matches the district's, so this is a fair comparison.

The projection is overstated by roughly 12–15%.

**3. The disposal saving and net cost are overstated (Sections 4 and 5).**
At £74/tonne, the corrected tonnage gives a saving of about £212,000–£217,000, not £243,000. The net annual cost rises from about £490,000 to about **£517,000–£521,000**. That is essentially equal to the whole £520,000 provisional allocation, leaving no headroom.

**4. Treatment capacity is not sufficient, and the cost of the shortfall is missing (Section 4).**
Brookfield can take up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029, but the study projects 2,900–3,300 tonnes. That leaves **1,100–1,500 tonnes a year** (35–45% of the total) for two years or more. The only alternative named is 46 miles away, with no gate fee or haulage cost given. The £74/tonne saving and the cost table both assume everything goes to Brookfield at £38 and 14 miles. The longer haul probably also needs more vehicle time, and possibly more vehicles or crews than the six costed. This gap needs to be quantified before the service can be called affordable.

## Significant issues

**5. "Fully funded" is overstated (Sections 5 and 7).**
The Government has "indicated" funding and the £520,000 is "provisional". Cabinet is being asked to commit to a £990,000 vehicle order on that basis. Also:
- The table shows depreciation, not cash. The capital outlay is up front and the study doesn't say how it will be financed.
- Once points 3 and 4 are corrected, the funding may not cover the net cost.
- There is no sensitivity analysis or fallback if the allocation is lower than expected.

**6. The resident feedback and contamination evidence is weaker than presented (Section 2).**
- The 81% satisfaction figure comes from *surveyed* households. Participants are likely over-represented, and non-participants, who are the main concern, may not have responded. Please give the response rate and the split by housing type.
- Contamination was checked in spot checks, with no sample size. Findings from a six-month pilot (January–June) may also not hold across summer, when food waste volumes and odour complaints change.

**7. The implementation timeline is tight (Section 6).**
Vehicles arrive in March, crews are trained that month, caddies reach about 52,000 households that month, and collections start on 5 April. There is no contingency for vehicle delivery delays, and the study doesn't say whether six vehicles can cover the district's rounds. A roll-out contingency or phased start would reduce the risk.

## Minor points
- Section 2 should state whether flats in the pilot used the same 23-litre outdoor caddy, since that may explain the low participation.
- The weighted average yield of 1.9 kg is correct, but it conceals the lower flat yield (1.4 kg). Use the split figures in the projection.
- Table 2 arithmetic checks out (£141,400 + £408,000 + £96,000 + £88,000 = £733,400), as do the 66%/21%/57% rates and the £74/tonne differential.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet
1. Correct the participation rate to 57% (or use the house/flat split) and recalculate tonnage, saving and net cost.
2. Replace the "uniform roll-out" conclusion with a flats strategy and cost it.
3. Add the cost of disposing of the tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800-tonne cap, including gate fee, haulage and any extra vehicle needs.
4. Present a funding scenario table (provisional allocation vs. lower) and set out the capital financing for the vehicles.
5. Reword the recommendation from "fully funded" to a conditional statement, or make the vehicle order conditional on confirmed funding.
